name: Akbar
info: Akbar (1542–1605), born Jalal-ud-Din Muhammad Akbar, was the third Mughal emperor, who reigned from 1556 to 1605, enlarged the empire across much of the Indian subcontinent and governed it through a centralised administration and religious conciliation.

facts.born: 15 October 1542 at the Rajput fortress of Amarkot (in modern-day Sindh); son of the exiled Mughal emperor Humayun and Hamida Banu Begum
facts.died: October 1605 (believed to have died on 26 October; also given as 27 October), after an attack of dysentery that began on 3 October; buried at his mausoleum in Sikandra, Agra
facts.role: Governor of Ghazni (appointed 1551); third Mughal emperor, proclaimed Shahanshah, 1556–1605, under the regency of Bairam Khan until 1560
facts.known: Enlarging the Mughal Empire across much of the Indian subcontinent; the mansabdari system of ranks; the dahsala land revenue system; alliances with the Rajputs; abolishing the sectarian tax; the Ibadat Khana debates and Din-i Ilahi; Fatehpur Sikri; the massacre at Chittor

t: Born in exile and enthroned at Kalanaur in 1556, Akbar secured the Mughal throne under his regent Bairam Khan, whom he dismissed in 1560.
By war, marriage and diplomacy he enlarged the empire to reach from the Bay of Bengal to Kandahar, and ordered it by ranked service and a land revenue assessed on ten-year averages.
He won the support of non-Muslim subjects through tolerance and high office, and moved from orthodox Islam to debates among all faiths, against the resistance of orthodox theologians.
dyk: Akbar never learned to read or write and is believed to have been dyslexic; he was read to every day, and he created a library of over 24,000 volumes, doing much of the cataloguing himself.
ev: Akbar is born at Amarkot, where his exiled parents had been given refuge by the Hindu ruler Rana Prasad
He succeeds Humayun in February, and in November his army under Bairam Khan defeats Hemu at the Second Battle of Panipat
He dismisses his regent Bairam Khan and orders him to leave on Hajj to Mecca
Chittorgarh falls after a siege of four months, and the defenders and 30,000 non-combatants are massacred
A victory near Ahmedabad in September completes the conquest of Gujarat
He builds the Ibadat Khana, the House of Worship, at Fatehpur Sikri for religious debates
Kabul becomes a Mughal province, and Akbar moves his capital to Lahore for thirteen years in the north
He falls ill with dysentery in October and dies; his son Prince Salim succeeds him as Jahangir

sections.early:
Akbar was born Jalal-ud-Din Muhammad Akbar on 15 October 1542 at the Rajput fortress of Amarkot, in modern-day Sindh, where his parents had been given refuge by the local Hindu ruler, Rana Prasad. His father, the Mughal emperor Humayun, had been defeated at Chausa in 1539 and at Kannauj in 1540 by the forces of Sher Shah Suri and had fled westward; there he married the 14-year-old Hamida Banu Begum.

During Humayun's long exile Akbar was brought up in Kabul by his paternal uncles Kamran Mirza and Askari Mirza and by his aunts. He spent his youth learning to hunt, run and fight; he never learned to read or write, but had someone read to him in the evenings. His childhood tutors, among them two Irani Shias, were largely above sectarian prejudice and contributed to his later inclination towards religious tolerance. In 1551, after his uncle Hindal Mirza died in battle against Kamran Mirza's forces, Humayun appointed the nine-year-old Akbar governor of Ghazni, gave him Hindal's retainers, lands and military command, and betrothed him to Hindal's daughter Ruqaiya Sultan Begum; they were married several years later, when both were about fourteen.

Humayun reconquered Delhi in 1555 with an army partly provided by his Persian ally Tahmasp I, and died a few months later. Akbar's guardian, Bairam Khan, concealed the death to prepare the succession. On 14 February 1556, in the midst of a war against Sikandar Shah to reclaim the Mughal throne, Akbar was enthroned by Bairam Khan at Kalanaur, Punjab, and was proclaimed Shahanshah, "King of Kings".
sections.rise:
Bairam Khan ruled on Akbar's behalf until he came of age. After Humayun's death the Surs reconquered Agra and Delhi, and Hemu proclaimed himself Hindu emperor and expelled the Mughals from the Indo-Gangetic Plains. Akbar's army, led by Bairam Khan, defeated Hemu and the Sur army on 5 November 1556 at the Second Battle of Panipat, and Mughal forces occupied Delhi and then Agra. Sikandar Shah Suri was beaten and fled to Bengal.

At eighteen Akbar wished to take a more active part in affairs. Urged on by his foster mother, Maham Anga, and other relatives, he dismissed Bairam Khan after a dispute at court in the spring of 1560 and ordered him to leave on Hajj to Mecca. Goaded into rebellion, Bairam Khan was defeated in the Punjab and forgiven; he resumed his pilgrimage and was assassinated on the way by a group of Afghans. In the conquest of Malwa that followed, Akbar's foster brother Adham Khan kept the spoils and slaughtered the surrendered garrison with their wives and children; Akbar rode to Malwa to relieve him of command. When Adham Khan confronted him after another dispute in late 1561, the emperor threw him from a terrace into the palace courtyard at Agra, and then a second time to ensure his death.

Akbar then distributed authority among specialised ministerial posts so that no one noble should become too powerful. He put down rebellions by a clan of Uzbek chiefs from 1564 and by the Mirzas, his distant cousins, and in 1566 turned back his brother Mirza Muhammad Hakim, ruler of Kabul, who had marched into the Punjab to seize the throne.
sections.deeds:
Akbar enlarged the Mughal Empire to include much of the Indian subcontinent. Chittor, the fortress-capital of Mewar, fell in February 1568 after a siege of four months, and Ranthambore soon after; most Rajput kings submitted, and many were bound to him by marriage alliances and rank at court. He occupied Ahmedabad in 1572 and secured Gujarat with a victory on 2 September 1573; Bengal was annexed after the Battle of Tukaroi in 1575. He seized Kabul in August 1581, and it became a province in 1585; Kashmir, Sindh, Baluchistan and Kandahar followed, and in the Deccan he took Ahmednagar Fort in August 1600 and Asirgarh on 17 January 1601.

Under the mansabdari system each officer held a rank, in 33 classes, and supplied a set number of cavalry. Land revenue, after earlier methods that burdened the peasantry and bred corruption among local officials, was assessed from 1580 by the dahsala system set out by Raja Todar Mal: one-third of the average produce of the previous ten years, paid in cash, with remission when harvests failed. In 1569 he founded a new capital, later called Fatehpur Sikri.

To keep peace in a religiously diverse empire he abolished the sectarian tax and appointed non-Muslims to high civil and military posts. In 1575 he built the Ibadat Khana, the "House of Worship", at Fatehpur Sikri, where Muslim theologians and later people of all religions debated. A declaration of 1579, signed by all the major ulema, asserted that he was the Khalifa of the age. He sought to combine the good practices of all religions in the movement known as Din-i Ilahi.
sections.opponents:
After the fall of Chittor Akbar had the surviving defenders and 30,000 non-combatants massacred and their heads displayed on towers throughout the region; he proclaimed the victory as that of "Islam over infidels". After the Gujarat rebellion of 1573 he slew the rebel leaders and built a tower of their severed heads; several leaders of the rebel Mirzas were trampled to death under elephants. Among the Rajputs, Udai Singh II of Mewar never submitted, and his son Maharana Pratap, defeated at Haldighati in 1576, kept most of his remaining kingdom.

His religious course made enemies among the Muslim orthodoxy. In his early reign he himself suppressed sects condemned as heretical, ordering in 1567 the exhumation of a Shia buried near a Sunni saint in Delhi. Later the debates at the Ibadat Khana shocked orthodox theologians, who circulated rumours that he wished to forsake Islam. In 1580 a rebellion broke out in the east and qazis issued fatwas declaring him a heretic, and in 1581 Muslim clerics rebelled to put his brother Mirza Muhammad Hakim on the throne; he suppressed both. The debates grew more acrimonious, and he ended them in 1582. The noble Aziz Koka wrote from Mecca in 1594 that the discipleship Akbar promoted amounted to no more than a desire to portray his superiority in religious matters.

In Pakistan his legacy is largely negative. The historian Ishtiaq Hussain Qureshi said that Akbar "had so weakened Islam through his policies that it could not be restored to its dominant position", and Pakistani historians commonly criticise his Rajput policy.
sections.last:
From 1585 Akbar remained in the north for thirteen years, with his capital at Lahore, dealing with the Uzbeks under Abdullah Khan Shaybanid, who had seized Badakhshan and Balkh, and with the Afghan tribes of the frontier. In 1586 he negotiated a pact with Abdullah Khan; an expedition against the Afghan tribes failed, and his minister Raja Birbal was ambushed and killed at the Malandarai Pass in February 1586. Abdullah Khan died in 1598, and the last of the rebellious Afghan tribes were subdued by 1600; despite a secret hope of reconquering Central Asia, Badakhshan and Balkh stayed in Uzbek hands. In 1599 he moved his capital back to Agra, where he ruled until his death.

His last campaigns were against the Deccan sultans, begun in 1593, after which he established the provinces of Ahmadnagar, Berar and Khandesh under Prince Daniyal. His son Prince Salim rebelled and then sought reconciliation, presenting his father with gold coins bearing Akbar's portrait.

On 3 October 1605 Akbar fell ill from an attack of dysentery, from which he never recovered. He is believed to have died on 26 October 1605; the date is also given as 27 October. He was buried at his mausoleum in Sikandra, Agra, a kilometre from the tomb of his favourite consort, Mariam-uz-Zamani. By the time of his death he controlled a broad sweep of territory from the Bay of Bengal to Kandahar and Badakshan. He was succeeded by Prince Salim, his first surviving son, born in 1569, later known as Jahangir. At his death there were no signs of discontent among his Muslim subjects.
sections.legacy:
Akbar firmly entrenched the authority of the Mughal Empire in India after it had been threatened by the Afghans in his father's reign. Under him Mughal India developed a strong and stable economy that tripled in size and wealth, and his courts at Delhi, Agra and Fatehpur Sikri became centres of the arts, letters and learning, where Timurid and Perso-Islamic culture blended with Indian elements into a distinct Mughal style in painting and architecture. The Rajputs became the strongest allies of the Mughals.

His son Jahangir and grandson Shah Jahan kept many of his concessions, such as the ban on cow slaughter, though Jahangir did not follow his tolerance towards the Jains. Whether Din-i Ilahi was a religion is disputed: some scholars argue that the idea arose from erroneous translations of Abul Fazl's work by British historians, and the historian M. Athar Ali wrote that sulh-e-kul, its essence, was adopted as part of general imperial administrative policy and formed the basis of Akbar's religious tolerance.

He is generally considered one of the greatest Mughal emperors. Time, citing a legacy of "pluralism and tolerance" that "underlies the values of the modern republic of India", included him in its list of top 25 world leaders. The historian Mubarak Ali has observed that in Pakistan Akbar "is conveniently ignored and not mentioned in any school textbook from class one to matriculation", and that he is criticised there for bringing Muslims and Hindus together as one nation, which contradicts the Two-Nation theory.

summary: Akbar (1542–1605), the third Mughal emperor, came to the throne in 1556 and enlarged the empire across much of the Indian subcontinent by conquest, marriage alliances and diplomacy. He built a centralised administration, abolished the sectarian tax and opened his court to debate among all faiths; his conquests included the massacre at Chittor in 1568.
references: Abul Fazl 'Allami, The Ain i Akbari (The Asiatic Society of Bengal, 1873)
Abul Fazl 'Allami, The Akbar Nama of Abu-l-Fazl (The Asiatic Society, 1907)
M. Athar Ali, Mughal India: Studies in Polity, Ideas, Society and Culture (Oxford University Press, 2006)
S. M. Burke, Akbar: The Greatest Mogul (Munshiram Manoharlal Publishers, 1989)
Allison Busch, Poetry of Kings: The Classical Hindi Literature of Mughal India (Oxford University Press, 2011)
notes: References: the saved article's Notes, References, Bibliography and Further reading sections are empty. The only work named with a date is in External links ('The Drama of Akbar by Muhammad Husain Azad from 1922'), so 1 reference, not 3-6; no publisher is given. Abul Fazl's Akbarnama and Ain-i-akbari and Jahangir's memoirs are named in the text as sources but without editions.

Death date: the lead gives 27 October 1605, the Death section 'believed to have died on 26 October 1605'. Both are given. Place of death is not stated outright (he 'ruled' from Agra 'until his death'; buried at Sikandra, Agra).
Age at accession: the article calls him 'the 14-year-old Akbar' in February 1556, though born 15 October 1542 (13 by that reckoning); I left the age out.
The marriage to Ruqaiya is 'in Jalandhar' in one passage and 'near Jalandhar' in another; place left out.

The Chittor victory dispatch (Fathnama) is dated '9 March 1575' in the article, seven years after the fall of the fort (probably an error for 1568); I left the dispatch's date and its 'destroyed the temples' quotation out and kept only 'the victory of Islam over infidels', which the article attributes to Akbar's proclamation.

Kandahar: one passage says it was secured in 1595 by a garrison under Shah Bayg Khan; another says it 'capitulated without resistance on 18 April 1595' (in a confused paragraph that also mentions Bairam Khan). I gave no date for it in the text.
'Abolishing the sectarian tax' is the lead's wording; the article does not name the jizya except for Jain pilgrim places, and gives no year for the abolition.
The article does not date Din-i Ilahi's promulgation (only the 1582 end of the debates and the 1583 renaming of Prayag); Oscar R. Gómez's 'transtheistic outlook' claim was left out.

Prince Salim's rebellion is mentioned only in the Coins section, without a date. The article gives almost nothing on Akbar's last years at court or the succession beyond 'succeeded by his son, Prince Salim'.
Badayuni is called 'Akbar's critic' but none of his criticisms is given, so he is not used.
Left out for length: the list of wives, relations with the Portuguese and Ottomans (Hajj caravans, cartaz), the Jain scholars at court, the language deprivation experiment, the tigress anecdote.
